Experimental design / conditions: 3.0 g rape straw in 100 mL DI water with FeSO4·7H2O 0.2 M, urea 0.5 M, ascorbic acid 0.14 M; ultrasonicate; dry 80 °C; pyrolyze 600 °C, 10 °C/min, 120 min under N2. Typical tests: 0.2 g/L, 50 mg/L each target, 298 K, 150 rpm.
Reported result: Fe/N-BC SBET = 20.35 m2/g; pore volume = 0.048 cm3/g. Fe/N incorporation assessed by EDX, XRD, FTIR and XPS.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2 / printed p. 387; preparation §2.1 and characterization §3.1
Evidence status: Extracted from main PDF; SI not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: No yield or preparation cost; exact characterization details partly in Supplementary Text S1.

Experimental design / conditions: Single-solute isotherm; dose 0.2 g/L; CIP 0–200 mg/L; pH 6.0 ± 0.2; temperatures 298, 308, 318 K.
Reported result: Langmuir fitted qmax = 25.36 (298 K), 39.20 (308 K), 46.45 (318 K) mg/g; respective R2 = 0.92, 0.89, 0.90. Freundlich fits had R2 0.99, 0.98, 0.99.
Model / metric: Langmuir qmax vs Freundlich fit; not observed qe
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 5 / printed p. 390; Table 2, Fig. 2 caption
Evidence status: Extracted; qmax explicitly identified as model-derived
Caveat / follow-up: Do not compare directly with fixed-condition uptake or column capacity; peak qmax occurs at 318 K.

Experimental design / conditions: Single-solute isotherm; dose 0.2 g/L; Cu2+ 0–100 mg/L; pH 6.0 ± 0.2; 298, 308, 318 K.
Reported result: Langmuir fitted qmax = 27.92, 28.35 and 30.77 mg/g at 298, 308 and 318 K; respective R2 = 0.94, 0.97 and 0.94.
Caveat / follow-up: Cu2+ is not an antibiotic; include only as co-contaminant/competition evidence.

Experimental design / conditions: Binary isotherms; CIP 0–200 mg/L and Cu2+ 0–100 mg/L; dose 0.2 g/L; pH 6.0 ± 0.2; 298–318 K.
Reported result: At 318 K, fitted Langmuir qmax fell to 18.84 mg/g for CIP and 17.23 mg/g for Cu2+. Increasing CIP concentration from 0 to 200 mg/L lowered Cu2+ uptake from 20.51 to 4.66 mg/g when Cu2+ was fixed.
Value / units: 18.84 mg/g CIP; 17.23 mg/g Cu2+; Cu uptake 20.51 to 4.66 mg/g
Model / metric: Binary-system fitted qmax and observed competition trend
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 5–6 / printed pp. 390–391; Table 2; §3.3.1–3.3.4; Fig. 3
Evidence status: Extracted; exact interpretation restricted to reported mixture
Caveat / follow-up: Competition is strong; binary and single-system values must remain separated.

Evidence domain: pH, ionic strength and water matrix
Experimental design / conditions: pH 2–6 and NaCl 0–100 mM; water-matrix test at 50 mg/L each in DI water, tap water and groundwater.
Reported result: Single system: CIP uptake highest around pH 5 at 20.20 mg/g; Cu2+ increased to 20.51 mg/g at pH 6. NaCl increased 0→100 mM: CIP 17.30→11.33 mg/g; Cu2+ 20.51→33.72 mg/g. Binary pH separation factors: SF(CIP) 7.42 at pH 2; SF(Cu2+) 0.14 at pH 2 and 3.82 at pH 6. Groundwater uptake 1.50× for CIP and 1.18× for Cu2+ vs DI; tap-water uptake slightly lower.
Value / units: As reported; units mg/g unless separation factor/fold-change
Model / metric: pH, ionic-strength, separation factor and matrix observations
Caveat / follow-up: Real-water tests are high-concentration spiked tap/groundwater, not real wastewater. Authors call CIP NaCl impact negligible although reported uptake changes by ~35%.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic tests at 298–318 K; 20 mg sorbent/100 mL, 50 mg/L target; at least triplicate; five sequential co-adsorption cycles.
Reported result: PSO frequently fitted better; XPS suggests changes in C–N, π–π*, C–O, M–O/C=O and Fe oxidation-state signals. Authors propose pore filling, π–π, electrostatics and H-bonding for CIP; iron-associated complexes/electrostatics for Cu2+. Cu2+ performance declines substantially after five cycles; CIP declines gradually.
Value / units: PSO R2 in single CIP tests 0.94–0.97; exact recycle values not captured from figure
Evidence status: Extracted with mechanism evidence rated indirect/proposed
Caveat / follow-up: PSO fit alone does not prove chemisorption; “reduction” of Cu requires verification from chemical-state evidence. No cost or regeneration-method detail.

Target / co-contaminant: CBZ, SMX, PAR (only SMX is antibiotic)
Experimental design / conditions: Dry primary paper-mill sludge + 50% ammonium lignosulfonate solution at 6:5 w/w; pyrolyze 500 °C 10 min under N2; KOH impregnate at 1:1 w/w; pyrolyze 800 °C 150 min under N2; acid/water wash; dry 105 °C 24 h; 0.5–1.0 mm granules.
Reported result: Virgin PSA-PA SBET = 671 m2/g, pore volume 0.37 cm3/g, DR micropore volume 0.27 cm3/g. Fixed bed 2.6 cm depth, ~3.56 g, 25 ± 1 °C; 5 mg/L feed; flow 4.3, 8.6 or 13.0 L/day in flow study.
Caveat / follow-up: Only SMX is an antibiotic; do not treat CBZ/PAR as antibiotic targets. Detailed preparation refers to prior article.

Evidence domain: Real wastewater / single and ternary feeds
Experimental design / conditions: Municipal biological WWTP effluent, filtered 0.45 μm; five campaigns March–June 2018; stored dark at 4 °C and used within 15 days; native target pharmaceuticals below detection, then spiked to 5 mg/L each. Wastewater pH ~7.3–7.7. Column flow 4.3 L/day; C/C0=0.1 threshold.
Reported result: Observed column qtotal in single wastewater solution: SMX 2.23 mg/g (t10%=0.10 d; breakthrough volume 0.45 L); CBZ 6.65 mg/g; PAR 4.46 mg/g. In ternary wastewater feed, SMX qtotal = 0.67 mg/g, CBZ 5.58 mg/g, PAR 8.57 mg/g.
Value / units: mg/g as integrated experimental column capacity; SMX values are antibiotic-relevant
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2, 5–7 / printed pp. 700, 703–705; §2.2–2.3; Table 1; Fig. 2
Caveat / follow-up: CBZ=antiepileptic, PAR=antidepressant. Breakthrough curves did not reach C/C0=1 within the test window; qtotal is not guaranteed true saturation capacity.

Experimental design / conditions: CBZ 5 mg/L; distilled water; flow rates 4.3, 8.6, 13.0 L/day; continuous fixed-bed.
Reported result: Observed qtotal = 39.91, 31.66, 19.95 mg/g and breakthrough time = 2.92, 0.83, 0.21 days, respectively. In wastewater at same flow rates, CBZ qtotal = 6.65, 7.00, 2.34 mg/g.
Model / metric: Observed integrated column values, not fitted qTH/qY
Caveat / follow-up: Distilled-water capacity is much higher than wastewater, consistent with matrix competition. CBZ is not antibiotic-specific evidence.

Experimental design / conditions: Exhausted PSA-PA after CBZ adsorption from distilled water; regenerate at 500 °C under N2 for 90 min; repeat fixed-bed adsorption at 4.3 L/day.
Reported result: CBZ qtotal: 39.91 mg/g virgin, 24.95 mg/g after first regeneration, 11.49 mg/g after second; SBET 671, 617 and 463 m2/g for cycles 0, 1 and 2; post-use cycle-2 area 391 m2/g.
Model / metric: Experimental column capacity and BET area
Caveat / follow-up: Authors recommend no more than one reuse cycle given thermal demand and capacity loss. No full energy/cost inventory.

Experimental design / conditions: Fitted Thomas, Yoon–Nelson and Yan models compared with experimental breakthrough curves.
Reported result: Example: CBZ in distilled water at 4.3 L/day, observed qtotal = 39.91 mg/g, Thomas qTH = 64.3 ± 1.2 mg/g and Yan qY = 59.6 ± 0.6 mg/g. Yan model generally fit best, but fitted capacities overestimate observed qtotal in several cases.
Value / units: mg/g; R2 per model in paper
Model / metric: Fitted model parameter vs experimentally integrated capacity
Caveat / follow-up: Curves often did not reach exhaustion; model predictions should not be substituted for measured integrated performance.

Adsorbent / material: KOH-activated dyeing-sludge biochar KSC-8; SC controls
Experimental design / conditions: Dewatered dyeing sludge (61.23% solids) dried 105 °C 72 h, ground 60 mesh; sludge:KOH 1:1 w/w; pyrolyze at 700/800/900 °C for 3 h, ramp 5 °C/min under N2; wash 3 M HCl for 6 h; rinse neutral, dry 75 °C overnight.
Reported result: SBET: unactivated SC-7/8/9 = 360.3/306.8/284.6 m2/g; activated KSC-7/8/9 = 791.2/1178.4/926.5 m2/g. KSC-8 pore volume = 0.74 cm3/g; pores described mostly <1 nm.
Caveat / follow-up: One sentence on PDF p. 7 prints 1078.4 m2/g while abstract, characterization and Table 2 show 1178.4 m2/g.

Experimental design / conditions: TC isotherm range 10–800 mg/L at 298 K; method describes 100 mL batch, shaker 180 rpm. Adsorbent mass/dose for batch tests is not clearly provided in main PDF.
Model / metric: Langmuir fitted qmax, not low-concentration observed uptake
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 6 / Table 1; §2.4 states isotherm concentrations and 298 K
Caveat / follow-up: Conclusion says 1081.3 mg/g at 278 K, while methods say isotherm tests at 298 K; SI needed. Do not rank without reporting dose and test concentration.

Experimental design / conditions: Temperature comparison with TC 100 mg/L; 298, 308 and 318 K. pH tests 3–11; KSC-8 pHpzc 4.4; TC pKa reported 3.3, 7.7, 9.7.
Reported result: Observed experimental uptake in temperature tests: 305.99 mg/g (298 K), 323.91 mg/g (308 K), 351.48 mg/g (318 K). Reported pH-5 uptake = 311.85 mg/g. PSO R2 = 0.997/0.999/0.996 vs PFO R2 = 0.910/0.937/0.913.
Model / metric: Observed qt,exp plus kinetic fits; condition details partly incomplete
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 6–7 / Fig. 3, Fig. 4; Table S5 referenced but not supplied
Evidence status: Extracted from main text; dose/SI pending
Caveat / follow-up: PSO fit is not proof of chemisorption; the reported dose for these batch conditions is not clear in supplied main PDF.

Experimental design / conditions: Simulated matrix: glucose 200 mg/L COD, NH4Cl to 30 mg/L ammonia-N and NaCl 300 mg/L chloride. Actual tailwater reported COD 57.19 mg/L, ammonia-N 0.40 mg/L. Main text reports TC completely removed within 30 min. A separate cross-antibiotic test used 20 mg/L for CIP, SMZ and tilmicosin in Methods.
Reported result: Reported removal: 100% TC, CIP and SMZ; 96.34% tilmicosin (Fig. 4e). Actual tailwater TC reportedly completely removed within 30 min; source and exact test composition need clarification.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not assume all four removal percentages are from real wastewater. Actual tailwater source, starting antibiotic concentrations and details are not fully described in main PDF.

Experimental design / conditions: Regeneration using 100 mL solution with Fe2+ 2 mM and H2O2 100 mM at initial pH 3 for 3 h; five cycles.
Reported result: Body text: by cycle 5 regeneration efficiency = 86.88% and retained adsorption capacity = 86.35%; cycles 1–3 retained 100% removal. Abstract calls 86.35% the removal efficiency after five cycles.
Model / metric: Regeneration efficiency vs retained capacity vs removal efficiency
Caveat / follow-up: Do not collapse the three differently labelled percentages. Fenton reagents and spent liquid need to be included in process-cost/end-of-life analysis.

Experimental design / conditions: Fixed-bed: 0.25 g KSC-8 in 100 × 16 mm cylindrical vessel (80 mL volume); influent TC 10 mg/L, pH 5; flow 1.5 mL/min; nominal dose 3.13 g/L; HRT around 50 min.
Reported result: 13.59 L treated before TC reached 1 mg/L; reported capacity at this threshold = 543.46 mg/g. Separately stated maximum fixed-bed capacity = 1124.2 mg/g.
Model / metric: Breakthrough endpoint vs reported maximum column capacity
Caveat / follow-up: The 1124.2 mg/g value exceeds batch Langmuir qmax of 1081.3 mg/g and is described as nearly equal despite being higher; verify capacity integration, run duration and definitions.

Experimental design / conditions: Author estimate: reagents ~$3/kg adsorbent; pyrolysis energy ~25 kWh and associated cost ~$5.6/kg; total preparation cost ~$9/kg; compared with asserted average activated-carbon cost ~$28/kg.
Reported result: Reported combined cost ~$9/kg, vs paper-referenced average AC ~$28/kg.
Value / units: USD/kg per paper; kWh amount basis unclear
Caveat / follow-up: Functional unit, year/currency basis, energy-price assumptions, yield, acid washing, wastewater treatment, equipment, scale, regeneration and spent-media costs are not established in the main PDF.

Experimental design / conditions: Mechanism discussion based on pHpzc/zeta potential, pore structure, FTIR/XPS and pH behaviour.
Reported result: Authors propose pore filling, electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions. Evidence is consistent with several interactions but does not quantify each contribution independently.
Model / metric: Proposed mechanism supported by characterization trends
Evidence status: Extracted; proposed mechanism not uniquely established
Caveat / follow-up: Paper's Eq. (2), PDF p. 3, prints removal R% = (C0−Ct)/Ct × 100; conventional formula uses C0 in denominator. Also temperature, BET area and regeneration labels conflict internally. Authors' removal/capacity calculations need confirmation.

Adsorbent / material: OTC-imprinted magnetic biochar (MBC@MIPs); MBC and non-imprinted MBC@NIPs controls
Experimental design / conditions: OTC template + methacrylic acid; EGDMA crosslinker; AIBN initiator. Deoxygenate, react at 60 °C for 24 h, magnetically separate, wash and vacuum-dry at 60 °C. Base MBC recipe refers to previous work/SI.
Reported result: SEM, FTIR, XRD, XPS, magnetic hysteresis and TGA support a polymer shell on magnetic biochar; authors report magnetic separation in under 10 s.
Evidence status: Extracted from main PDF; SI not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: Base-biochar recipe/yield and some characterization details are not fully present; no cost/energy inventory.

Experimental design / conditions: Dosage: 5 mg/L OTC, 25 °C, pH 6.50 ± 0.1; 0.1–1.0 g/L. pH test: 0.5 g/L, 5 mg/L OTC at 25 °C.
Reported result: Removal rose from 17.0% at 0.1 g/L to 89.37% at 0.5 g/L; 1.0 g/L gave marginal further gain. Removal at pH 6.34 ~89.4%, pH 3 41.6%, pH 10 26.8%.
Evidence status: Extracted from figure/caption and main text
Caveat / follow-up: Lab water only; not real wastewater. Removal is condition-specific, not capacity.

Experimental design / conditions: 0.5 g/L adsorbent, 2 mg/L OTC, 25 °C, pH 6.50 ± 0.1; 250 rpm; 6 h.
Reported result: For MBC@MIPs: PFO fitted qe 10.84 mg/g (R² 0.9805); PSO fitted qe 12.55 mg/g (R² 0.9995); narrative reports experimental uptake about 12.07 mg/g. About 70–90% uptake within 4 h.
Model / metric: Kinetic model-fitted capacities vs experimental uptake
Caveat / follow-up: PSO is a statistical fit, not proof of chemisorption; prose mixes mg/g and mg/L in places.

Experimental design / conditions: OTC isotherms span 1–200 mg/L. Abstract quotes 299 K; methods generally say 25 °C.
Reported result: MBC@MIPs Langmuir fitted qmax 67.89 mg/g (R² 0.9821); narrative gives experimental 60.19 mg/g at a cited condition. Table 2 lists MBC 38.34 mg/g but abstract/body report 38.84 mg/g; BC 8.96 mg/g; MBC@NIPs 41.09 mg/g.
Model / metric: Fitted qmax vs reported experimental uptake
Caveat / follow-up: Do not silently choose 38.34 vs 38.84 mg/g; check SI/curve for experimental uptake condition.

Target / co-contaminant: OTC, DOX, TC, CTC, NOR, MNZ; competing antibiotics
Experimental design / conditions: Individual test: 0.5 g/L, 4 mg/L antibiotic, 25 °C, 6 h; mixed antibiotic condition shown in Fig. 4.
Reported result: Individual uptake: OTC 11.97 mg/g; TC 4.01; DOX 7.28. Imprinting factors: OTC 5.64, DOX 2.93, TC 2.95, CTC 4.14, NOR 1.05, MNZ 1.34. In mixture, OTC uptake 6.10 mg/g and IF 6.70.
Caveat / follow-up: Reported OTC 11.97 mg/g exceeds mass-balance ceiling of 8 mg/g implied by Fig. 4a conditions (C0=4 mg/L; dose=0.5 g/L). Treat as unresolved and do not use for quantitative comparison. Controlled mixtures only, not real wastewater; IF is distinct from capacity/removal.

Experimental design / conditions: Seven reuse cycles. Leaching protocol: 100 mg sorbent in 10 mL DI water for 24 h at pH 2–9; iron assessed by graphite-furnace AAS.
Reported result: Authors report 9.36% reduction in OTC binding over seven cycles. Leaching protocol is described but numerical iron results are not given in the accessible main-text details.
Model / metric: Reuse stability; leaching result not captured
Evidence status: Partial evidence; precise cycle values graphical; iron result unresolved
Caveat / follow-up: No real wastewater, column, cost estimate or numeric leaching result in main PDF.

Adsorbent / material: Bacterial-cellulose microfilament char / chitosan / polyethyleneimine crosslinked beads
Continuum stage: Stage 2/3 interface — biopolymer-based composite with hydrothermal char
Experimental design / conditions: Cellulose membrane hydrolysed with cold 64% H2SO4; 4 g filaments dispersed in 50 mL water, sonicated 1 h, pH 2, hydrothermal treatment 200 °C for 18 h (10 °C/min). Beads: 100 mL 1% chitosan in 2% acetic acid, PEI 1:1 molar ratio, 0.2 g char, 3 mL of 1% GA, drop into 1 M NaOH, wash/freeze-dry.
Reported result: A millimetre-scale crosslinked composite bead integrates char within the CS/PEI matrix.
Caveat / follow-up: No bead/char yield, energy inventory or preparation cost; some prior-method details/SI unavailable.

Adsorbent / material: BCM char/CS/PEI beads; PEI/CS bead and char controls
Experimental design / conditions: N2 adsorption, FTIR, EDX, SEM/TEM, TGA and zeta potential; beads 1.5–2 mm.
Reported result: BET area: PEI/CS 5.98 m²/g; BCM char 112.42 m²/g; composite beads 89.81 m²/g. Composite BJH pore volume 0.0991 cm³/g; C/O/N 44.95/27.05/28.00%; isoelectric point 9.3 for beads, 2.6 for char.
Caveat / follow-up: Reported pore-size around 68.4 Å is described as “sub-micropores”; terminology requires checking before repetition.

Experimental design / conditions: Typical time experiment: 4 mg in 15 mL (~0.267 g/L), 50 mg/L antibiotic, 298 K, pH 8 for TET and 6 for MET; pH tests from 3 to 9.
Reported result: At 10 mg/L and 90 min, abstract reports TET removal 99.13% and MET 90%; body reports TET 99.52% and MET 90%. TET pH optimum 8; MET pH optimum 6.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not choose 99.13% vs 99.52% silently. No real-water matrix experiment in main text.

Experimental design / conditions: Optimized condition in conclusion: 4 mg adsorbent in 15 mL (~0.267 g/L), 90 min, initial concentration 400 mg/L, 298 K; pH 8 TET/pH 6 MET.
Reported result: Empirical capacities 960.778 mg/g TET and 691.325 mg/g MET.
Model / metric: Empirical uptake at high starting concentration
Caveat / follow-up: Capacities are at 400 mg/L initial concentration, not environmental trace concentration.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic time series: 4 mg in 15 mL of 50 mg/L solution, optimal pH, 298 K. PFO, PSO, Avrami, Elovich, Bangham, IPD and LFD models compared.
Reported result: Table 2: PFO qcal 411.702 mg/g TET (R² .937) and 381.495 MET (.942); PSO qcal 204.081 TET (.998) and 188.67 MET (.992). Text reports practical kinetic uptake around 186 mg/g TET and 158 mg/g MET; staged Avrami fit R² up to .999.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–9; Table 2 and Fig. S7 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Do not mix these 50 mg/L kinetic values with 400 mg/L isotherm capacities. Multiple models fit; model fit alone does not prove mechanism.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherms cover initial concentrations 10–400 mg/L; Langmuir, Freundlich, Temkin, Redlich–Peterson, Sips, Toth and others fitted.
Reported result: Table 3 Langmuir qmax,cal 990.099 mg/g TET (R² .996) and 666.66 MET (.997); Sips 918.26/.987 and 690.59/.985; Toth 880/.963 and 790/.991. Empirical values in conclusion are 960.778/691.325 mg/g.
Caveat / follow-up: Several isotherms fit well; keep model-derived and observed values distinct.

Experimental design / conditions: Mechanisms interpreted from pH/zeta potential and FTIR/EDX; regeneration uses repeated water/methanol washing. Article refers to 11 cycles but also gives metrics “over two cycles.”
Reported result: Authors propose electrostatic, π–π, hydrogen-bond and Lewis acid–base interactions. Conflicting regeneration: TET removal 96.7%→89.81% “over two cycles” and 92.86% total effectiveness, but elsewhere says removal reaches 63.22% after eleven cycles (65.37% of starting value).
Caveat / follow-up: Do not quote one settled 11-cycle retention value; the article notes solvent/post-treatment cost, bead stability and spent-media disposal.

Target / co-contaminant: AZ, CPX, SMX, TMP, TC; nutrients
Adsorbent / material: Sewage-sludge biochar at 550/700 °C; CAS or DMSO surface modification
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — solvent/chemical modified biochar; source-separated urine application
Experimental design / conditions: SS550/SS700 biochars supplied by UK Biochar Research Centre; modification screened across DMSO, ionic liquids and DES. Selected variants include SS550/SS700 CAS and SS550/SS700 DMSO. Exact pyrolysis and modifier recipes reference SI.
Reported result: SS700 pristine BET 32.21 m²/g; after modification 16.99 m²/g (CAS) and 20.27 m²/g (DMSO). Mean pore diameter 5.03 nm pristine, 5.67 nm CAS, 7.37 nm DMSO. Contact angles across samples 14.12–66.41°; modified chars more hydrophilic.
Caveat / follow-up: Modification reduces BET area while increasing mean pore diameter/hydrophilicity; full recipe/yield/cost absent from main text.

Adsorbent / material: CAS/DMSO-modified sewage-sludge biochar; later stage uses separate pristine char for nutrients
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — modified biochar; source-separated urine application
Experimental design / conditions: Fresh human urine diluted 1:1 with DI water to imitate flushed urine; antibiotics spiked. Isotherms: 20 mL, dose 0.1–20 g/L, each antibiotic 100 or 1000 µg/L, 30±1 °C, 180 rpm, 24 h. Kinetics: 5 g/L, 100–1000 µg/L. pH tests: 40 mg/40 mL, each antibiotic 25 µg/L, pH 3–11, 24 h.
Reported result: Triplicate experiments; kinetic figure uses pH 7. Stage 1 modified char targets antibiotics; separate pristine char used in stage 2 for nutrients.
Caveat / follow-up: Diluted, spiked human urine is a special source-separated matrix, not municipal wastewater effluent or untreated urine with native target concentrations.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm tests used µg/L-scale initial concentrations; Langmuir/Freundlich compared with Temkin and Redlich–Peterson.
Reported result: Reported cross-material maximum capacities: AZ 196.08 µg/g (SS700 CAS); TMP 370.37 µg/g (SS700 CAS); TC 833.33 µg/g (SS550 DMSO); SMX about 81 µg/g (SS700 DMSO); CPX about 263 µg/g (SS550 CAS).
Model / metric: Reported maximum/fitted capacities across selected variants
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1, 5–6; abstract and §3.3.1; Table S6 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Values at µg/L feed concentrations are not directly comparable to mg/L-scale capacity studies.

Target / co-contaminant: AZ, TMP, TC, SMX, CPX; ammonia/phosphate comparators
Experimental design / conditions: Table 1 gives SS700 CAS and SS700 results; global R² ranges for Langmuir/Freundlich are 0.42–0.99 and 0.51–0.99.
Reported result: SS700 CAS Langmuir Qm (µg/g): AZ 196.08, TMP 370.37, TC −151.52, SMX 80.00, CPX 120.48. Pristine SS700 Qm negative for all five antibiotics. SS700 CAS phosphate Qm also negative (−7.06 mg/g).
Caveat / follow-up: Negative fitted capacities are physically unusable; indicate poor model fit for those pairs and should not be listed as real capacities.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetics at 5 g/L and pH 7 in Fig. 2; antibiotics 100–1000 µg/L. pH tests at 25 µg/L each, pH 3–11, 24 h, 30±1 °C.
Reported result: Authors report SS700 CAS antibiotic equilibrium at ~12 h; PSO R² range 0.68–0.99; Elovich R² 0.94–0.99. Adsorption strongest around pH 7. The separate nutrient stage reports ammonia uptake up to 60 mg N/g on SS550 biochar; phosphate adsorption low.
Value / units: µg/g antibiotic scale; mg N/g nutrient capacity
Model / metric: Kinetics, pH and separate nutrient uptake
Caveat / follow-up: Authors propose H-bonding, electrostatics and π–π interactions; these contributions are not separately quantified. Keep nutrient and antibiotic metrics separate.

Target / co-contaminant: AZ, CPX, SMX, TMP, TC; ammonia/phosphate
Experimental design / conditions: Loading: pH 7, 24 h, 1000 µg/L antibiotic, 5 g/L char, 30±1 °C. Regenerate with isopropanol at 5–20 g char/L IPA, 180 rpm for 24 h; five cycles.
Reported result: After cycle 5, CPX/TMP regeneration efficiencies <20%; AZ/SMX/TC roughly 40–50%. Authors advise not using regenerated char beyond three cycles. Phosphate was not extracted after cycle 2 in this procedure.
Caveat / follow-up: Abstract says <30% removal capacity after three cycles while body gives antibiotic-specific values after five cycles; preserve metric/time discrepancy. No solvent recovery/cost/LCA.

Experimental design / conditions: Stage 1 uses solvent-modified biochar for antibiotic capture; stage 2 uses separate pristine biochar for nutrient recovery from the remaining solution.
Reported result: Paper reports about 90% removal of antibiotics in stage 1. Some nutrient adsorption occurs in stage 1; stage 2 is designed for later nutrient capture. No full process-cost, solvent-recovery, energy inventory or LCA provided.
Caveat / follow-up: This is urine treatment rather than wastewater-effluent treatment. DMSO/DES/IL modification and isopropanol regeneration must be included in process sustainability analysis.

Experimental design / conditions: Scopus and ScienceDirect; base terms antibiotics and adsorption combined with clays, water, adsorbents, wastewater, modified-clays and bionanocomposites. Excluded pre-2000 and non-English papers.
Reported result: Review reports 6,208 initial records, 250 after adding “clays”, 90 candidates screened and 82 final studies; 45% natural clays and 55% modified/combined clays.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2 / printed p. 2; §2 Search strategy
Evidence status: Extracted from review PDF; supplementary Table S1 not retrieved
Caveat / follow-up: Secondary review counts, not our own search; review coverage ends around 2021, not a current 2026 count.

Adsorbent / material: Natural minerals: MMT, KAOL, BENT, SEP, illite, STV and others
Experimental design / conditions: Review-cited examples combine differing pH, feed concentrations and fitted models; each primary source needs rechecking.
Reported result: CIP on Ca-MMT SAz-1: 330 mg/g at C0 500–4,000 mg/L; Na-MMT at pH 5.5: CTC 79.97, OTC 33.15, TC 49.78 mg/g; tetracycline on SWy-2/SAz-1/RECT 355/460/140 mg/g (C0 100–3,000 mg/L); SEP: marbofloxacin 132 and enrofloxacin 112 mg/g (C0 20–1,800 mg/L); STV: TC/OTC/CTC 127.1/126.1/139.9 mg/g (C0 50–1,000 mg/L).
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4–5 / printed pp. 4–5; §§4.1–4.6; Table S4 cited
Evidence status: Secondary evidence; not independently verified against all originals
Caveat / follow-up: Not a homogeneous ranking; mineral source, pH, feed, dose and model differ.

Adsorbent / material: Modified clay, biochar–clay, pillared clay, hybrid silicate and LDH composites
Experimental design / conditions: Examples cited: carboxymethyl-chitosan–MMT, wheat-straw MMT–biochar, Si/Fe-pillared bentonite, hybrid silicate from palygorskite, calcined bentonite and MgAl-LDH/carbon composites.
Reported result: Review quotes carboxymethyl-chitosan–MMT: TC 178.57 and CTC 271.74 mg/g (C0 5–400 mg/L); MMT-biochar vs raw biochar: NOR 25.53 vs 10.58 mg/g (C0 0.4–15 mg/L); Si/Fe-pillared bentonite: CIP 100.6/122.1 mg/g (C0 18–500 mg/L); hybrid silicate: CTC 329.84 and OTC 207.47 mg/g (C0 50–800 mg/L).
Value / units: mg/g and C0 conditions as cited
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 5–6 / printed pp. 5–6; §4.7; Table S5 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Processing cost and test conditions differ; modification does not automatically outperform raw material in every context.

Experimental design / conditions: Review synthesizes mechanisms as dependent on antibiotic speciation, clay surface charge/structure, pH, co-ions and salinity.
Reported result: Possible interactions include cation exchange, cation bridging/complexation, electrostatic attraction/repulsion, hydrogen bonding, π interactions, hydrophobic/London forces and interlayer filling. Review explicitly warns PSO/PFO kinetic fits alone do not establish chemo-/physisorption; use FTIR, SEM/TEM, IEP/PZC, Raman, NMR, XRD and/or XPS alongside adsorption observations.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–10 / printed pp. 7–10; §§4.8–4.10 and Fig. 2
Caveat / follow-up: IEP and PZC are different measurements; do not treat them as interchangeable.

Evidence domain: Review’s literature window ends around 2021; SI tables not available in the supplied PDF.
Experimental design / conditions: Authors counted 15/82 studies with real wastewater tests, seven continuous-flow studies and no pilot-scale studies in their review window. Ampicillin performance reportedly fell from 89.9% to 59.3% for bentonite and from 100% to 90.6% for CTAB-bentonite when moving from synthetic to pharmaceutical-company wastewater. Historical cost snapshots: MMT US$40–120/t, bentonite US$74/t, GAC US$1,000/t, CNT US$12,000–90,000/t, Ti-PILC US$9,500/t.
Reported result: Counts, removal percentages and historic US$/ton estimates
Value / units: Review synthesis / practical gap / cost snapshots
Model / metric: PDF pp. 6, 10–11 / printed pp. 6, 10–11; §§4.7, 4.11–4.12 and conclusion
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): Secondary evidence; current costs not independently verified
Evidence status: Historical review counts are not 2026 field counts; price year, location, grade and scale not specified; LCA reported missing in reviewed studies.

Experimental design / conditions: 0.2 g clay + 20 mL CIP; 150 rpm, 24 h, dark-wrapped tubes. Isotherm C0 500–4,000 mg/L; pH-edge C0 3,000 mg/L, pH 2.5–11 adjusted with 1 M HCl/NaOH; experiments in duplicate.
Reported result: SAz-1 is a Ca2+-dominated swelling montmorillonite; BET external area 65.2 m²/g and CEC 123 meq/100 g (1.23 meq/g). Supernatant separated by centrifugation, filtered at 0.45 μm and analysed by UV/Vis at 275 nm.
Caveat / follow-up: High-concentration batch study; no kinetics, reuse, real-water or continuous-flow testing.

Experimental design / conditions: C0 500–4,000 mg/L; 0.2 g in 20 mL; 150 rpm, 24 h; acidic/neutral solutions.
Reported result: Reported capacity 330 mg/g (1.0 mmol/g), Langmuir R² 0.9997 versus Freundlich R² 0.8744. At C0 3,000 mg/L, Ce = 80 mg/L, equivalent to about 97.33% removal and ~292 mg/g observed uptake. Keep 330 fitted/reported capacity distinct from the ~292 mg/g observed condition.
Model / metric: Reported maximum/model capacity vs observed uptake
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 3 / printed p. 311; Fig. 2 and §3.1
Evidence status: Extracted from primary PDF; isotherm figure visually checked
Caveat / follow-up: Feed range far above trace wastewater concentrations; not evidence by itself for low-concentration treatment.

Experimental design / conditions: pH-edge experiments at C0 3,000 mg/L, with pH adjusted 2.5–11. Reported CIP pKa1 ≈ 6.1 and pKa2 ≈ 8.7; clay remains negatively charged over the tested range.
Reported result: Uptake stayed near 290–300 mg/g from pH 2.8–8.8 and decreased to 247 mg/g at pH 11. Authors attribute the decline above pKa2 to repulsion of anionic CIP from negative clay surfaces.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 4 / printed p. 312; Fig. 4 and §3.2
Caveat / follow-up: High-feed single-solute test; do not extrapolate absolute uptake to real wastewater.

Target / co-contaminant: CIP and displaced interlayer cations (mainly Ca2+)
Experimental design / conditions: Ion chromatography measured released Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+; XRD measured d001 spacing; FTIR compared pure CIP and clay loaded to 292 mg/g at C0 3,000 mg/L.
Reported result: Total cation release versus CIP uptake slope ≈0.99 with near-zero intercept (y = −0.05 + 0.99x; R² = 0.9935); Ca2+ was the main released cation. d001: 15.04 Å raw → 14.62 Å at <150 mg/g → 17.23 Å above 290 mg/g. FTIR bands shifted 1624→1628 cm−1 and 1385→1390 cm−1; bands at 1582/1379 cm−1 were assigned to carboxylate.
Model / metric: Stoichiometric evidence plus XRD/FTIR; ~35° orientation is proposed model
Evidence status: Strong support for cation exchange under the tested conditions
Caveat / follow-up: Molecular orientation is an inference from XRD/FTIR, not a direct molecular image; no real-water or competition study.

Experimental design / conditions: Batch only; duplicate tests; C0 500–4,000 mg/L; UV/Vis 275 nm with reported calibration 0–10 mg/L, R² >0.99.
Reported result: Provides strong mechanistic evidence but no real wastewater, kinetic model, regeneration/reuse, fixed-bed operation, cost, yield or lifecycle study. Main text does not explain dilution of residual concentrations that exceed the stated calibration range.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–6 / printed pp. 310–314; Methods and Conclusions
Caveat / follow-up: Keep the high-concentration study separate from trace-level wastewater evidence; note the unexplained analytical dilution detail only if reconstructing the method.

Adsorbent / material: Cotton-husk H3PO4-activated biochar (PCH); unactivated CH control
Experimental design / conditions: 10 g cotton husk, 15 mL H3PO4 at 10–40%; stir 15 min; pyrolyse 120 min at 300–700 °C, ramp 5 °C/min under N2 0.1 L/min; wash to neutral pH, dry 80 °C, grind <0.2 mm. Selected PCH: 30% H3PO4, 600 °C. CH control: 600 °C without acid.
Reported result: One-step acid activation; paper provides selected temperature/concentration route but no product yield or full process mass balance.
Caveat / follow-up: Acid consumption per kg product, wash-water demand and spent-acid treatment are not reported in the main text.

Experimental design / conditions: BET, N2 adsorption, SEM, FTIR, XRD, XPS and pHpzc were measured; average pore size cited as 8.2 nm.
Reported result: PCH BET surface area 316.1 m²/g; pore volume 0.45 cm³/g vs CH pore volume 0.19 cm³/g; PCH pHpzc 2.57; phosphorus-oxygen groups including O–P and C–P–O reported.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3–4 and 7–8; Figs. 2–3, 6–7; Table S2 cited
Evidence status: Extracted from main text; SI not retrieved
Caveat / follow-up: Production yield and complete characterization values for CH are partly SI-dependent.

Experimental design / conditions: 10 mg PCH in 100 mL solution (0.1 g/L), pH 6, 120 rpm; C0 30, 60, 120 mg/L; sample 5–720 min.
Reported result: Equilibrium reached in about 4 h. Experimental uptake: 281.4 mg/g at C0 30 mg/L, 410.4 at 60 mg/L, 599.8 at 120 mg/L. PSO fitted values: 279.2, 407.2, 592.2 mg/g (R² 0.997, 0.998, 0.999).
Model / metric: Observed Qe vs PSO fitted Qe
Caveat / follow-up: PSO fit does not itself establish chemisorption; note high C0 and 0.1 g/L dose.

Experimental design / conditions: C0 20–160 mg/L, 10 mg PCH/100 mL (0.1 g/L), pH 6, 12 h; temperatures 288, 298, 308 K.
Reported result: Table 3: at 288 K, measured Qe 524.1 mg/g and Langmuir fitted Qm 496.4 (R² 0.973); at 298 K, measured Qe 572.8 and fitted Qm 523.0 (R² 0.957); at 308 K, measured Qe 621.4 and fitted Qm 572.8 (R² 0.982).
Model / metric: Measured Qe distinctly separated from Langmuir Qm
Caveat / follow-up: Abstract labels 572.8 mg/g as maximum capacity at 25 °C, but table labels 572.8 as measured Qe at 298 K and fitted Qm at 308 K. Do not merge these metrics.

Target / co-contaminant: CIP; coexisting Na+, K+, NO3−, SO4²−, Ca²+, Mg²+, CO3²−
Experimental design / conditions: pH tests 2–10; pHpzc 2.57; co-ion tests use CIP C0 30–120 mg/L, 0.1 g/L, 6 h, pH 6, 15–35 °C; dose tests include 0.05–0.2 g/L.
Reported result: Reported capacity around 295.2 mg/g at pH 6. Na+, K+, NO3− and SO4²− had minor effects; Ca²+/Mg²+ caused ~12% inhibition; CO3²− caused 17.8%, 22.7%, 25.9% inhibition at increasing tested levels. Dose section reports 94.17% removal at 0.1 g/L and only ~5.4% added removal on raising dose to 0.2 g/L.
Caveat / follow-up: Figure caption groups C0 values as 30–120 mg/L; exact starting concentration for every dose-screen value is not unambiguously stated in prose.

Target / co-contaminant: Bulk organics/color in real pharmaceutical secondary effluent; target-specific CIP not reported
Experimental design / conditions: Secondary pharmaceutical wastewater, pH unadjusted; 1 g/L PCH, stirred 120 rpm for 2 h. EEM fluorescence, CODCr and TOC measured before/after.
Reported result: CODCr declined 486.45→50.14 mg/L; TOC 71.63→21.33 mg/L; fluorescence intensity reduced/disappeared and effluent color changed from brown to transparent.
Caveat / follow-up: This is real-matrix evidence for bulk organic-load/color reduction, not quantified CIP-specific removal: initial/remaining CIP concentrations are not reported.

Experimental design / conditions: Three-cycle adsorption-desorption experiment compared EtOH, 2 M HCl and 2 M NaOH.
Reported result: Reported cycle-3 capacities 150.33, 156.49 and 196.96 mg/g, stated as 54.04%, 56.25% and 70.79% of control, respectively. Text says acid/base desorption was less desirable than EtOH, but prose-to-route ordering is ambiguous.
Caveat / follow-up: Preserve values and flag ambiguity; do not assert a definitive desorption-agent ranking until SI/figure mapping is confirmed.

Experimental design / conditions: Author cost model and comparator are reported with details in SI Table S4, not supplied in the uploaded PDF.
Reported result: Authors report PCH preparation cost US$3.98/kg vs cited commercial activated carbon US$259.5/kg, and an expected cost of US$7.64 per kg CIP treated/adsorbed.
Value / units: US$/kg adsorbent; US$/kg CIP as paper-described
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–9; §3.4; SI Table S4 cited
Evidence status: Main-text values extracted; cost assumptions unresolved
Caveat / follow-up: Not a harmonized TEA or current market quote; process yield, energy price, scale, washing-water/acid treatment, equipment, labor, regeneration and disposal boundaries unclear.

Adsorbent / material: PCH functional groups / O–P, C–P–O, C–O, –OH
Experimental design / conditions: FTIR/XPS before/after adsorption; DFT/ESP and Mulliken/adsorption-energy comparisons for functional groups.
Reported result: Authors propose pore filling, electrostatics, hydrogen bonding and π–π EDA interactions. Calculated adsorption energies (paper reports negative values): O–P −1.113 eV, C–P–O −0.635, C–O −0.425, –OH −0.327, CH −0.261. O–P is predicted as most favorable, particularly for hydrogen bonding.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–9; Figs. 6–7; SI Tables S5–S6 cited
Caveat / follow-up: DFT shows modelled relative interactions, not direct measured fractional contributions of each mechanism.

Adsorbent / material: Pristine macadamia nutshell biochar (MBC; paper abbreviation)
Experimental design / conditions: Shells washed, sun-dried 48 h; pyrolyse at 600 °C for 2 h under N2 0.3 L/min, ramp 10 °C/min; wash to pH 7; particle size 125–500 μm; dry 105 °C for 6 h.
Reported result: BET area ≈392 m²/g; total pore volume ≈0.18 cm³/g; micropore volume ≈0.05 cm³/g; DFT pore diameter ≈1.17 nm; EDS C 85.4±0.2%, O 14.5±0.2%; Raman ID/IG=2.68.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–5; §§2.1–2.2, 3.1; Fig. 1; Table S2 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Abbreviation MBC means macadamia biochar in this paper, not magnetic biochar. Product yield/cost and complete material data in SI not retrieved.

Experimental design / conditions: Each antibiotic C0=4 mg/L, adsorbent 8 g/L, pH 7, 20±1 °C, 120 rpm; sample times 2–1440 min; concentrations normalized to mmol/L.
Model / metric: Bayesian posterior means for PSO model parameters
Caveat / follow-up: Units are mmol/kg rather than mg/g. High dose 8 g/L and low C0=4 mg/L; not directly comparable with studies using much lower doses.

Experimental design / conditions: C0 4–60 mg/L, dose 8 g/L, pH 7, 20 °C, dark, 120 rpm, ~600 min; models use C normalized to mmol/L.
Model / metric: Fitted Bayesian Langmuir Qmax, not observed kinetic qe
Caveat / follow-up: Do not mix model-derived Qmax with Table 1 kinetic qe or convert units without preserving assumptions and molecular weights.

Experimental design / conditions: MBC pHpzc ≈6.3; pH 3, 7, 10 isotherm comparisons; FTIR, PCA/HCA chemometrics and Bayesian parameter distributions.
Reported result: Sorption trend reported CFX > TMP > OFX > SMX. Authors propose H-bonding, π–π EDA interactions, electrostatic effects and mesopore/external-surface filling; pH/speciation substantially changes Langmuir parameter distributions.
Caveat / follow-up: No real wastewater, columns, regeneration, cost, leaching, or LCA. Mechanisms are proposed from indirect evidence/model patterns, not individually quantified.

Evidence domain: Adsorption setup and measured kinetic uptake
Experimental design / conditions: 0.02 g adsorbent + 20 mL TC at 25 mg/L, pH 7, 100 rpm, 25 °C; 1 g/L dose. Isotherms use C0 10–120 mg/L, 24 h, 298–328 K.
Reported result: At 298 K, observed uptake: Sep 11.252 mg/g, Mt 20.736 mg/g. Approximate equilibration: 240 min Sep, 120 min Mt. At 308/318 K, observed values: Sep 11.721/11.958 mg/g; Mt 21.815/22.564 mg/g.
Caveat / follow-up: These observed kinetic values are not the fitted isotherm Qmax values from Table 4.

Experimental design / conditions: Same kinetic design: 25 mg/L TC, 1 g/L adsorbent, pH 7, 100 rpm, 298/308/318 K.
Reported result: PSO fitted Qe values approximate experiment with R²=0.997–0.999. PFO R² is about 0.789–0.897. Authors interpret this as chemical adsorption, but fit quality alone does not establish chemisorption.
Caveat / follow-up: Use model fit as descriptive evidence, not stand-alone mechanism proof.

Experimental design / conditions: C0 10–120 mg/L, 1 g/L adsorbent, pH 7, 24 h, 298–328 K.
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir Qmax, separate from observed 25 mg/L uptake
Caveat / follow-up: Qmax is fitted across the isotherm concentration series and must not be substituted for experimental uptake at C0=25 mg/L.

Experimental design / conditions: pH tests 3–11; pHpzc reported ≈6.4 for Sep and ≈2.5 for Mt; TC pKa values cited as 3.30, 7.68, 9.69. Ionic-strength experiments use K+, Na+, Ca2+, Mg2+.
Reported result: TC capacity fell as pH increased; Mt outperformed Sep across tested pH and dose. K+/Na+ had relatively little influence; Ca2+/Mg2+ inhibited adsorption more. Authors propose hydrogen bonding, van der Waals, electrostatics and cation exchange/bridging; XRD d001 for Mt changed 1.460 nm raw → 1.515 nm after TC → 1.465 nm after MW regeneration.
Caveat / follow-up: No real wastewater/co-contaminant pharmaceutical matrix was tested.

Experimental design / conditions: Spent material dried at 75 °C to constant weight, irradiated at 750 W for 5–45 min; selected time 25 min Sep and 20 min Mt. Nominal power×time = 0.3125 and 0.25 kWh per exposure, respectively (calculated, not measured).
Reported result: At selected times: Fig. 15 regeneration ratio Sep 81.83% at 25 min; Mt 98.83% at 20 min. Cycle series (Fig. 17): Sep reaches 89.76% by cycle 4, declines to 65.21% at cycle 8; Mt 98.56% in cycle 1 and 66.38% at cycle 8. Abstract/conclusion reports maximum ratios 89.76% Sep and 114.45% Mt under optimized conditions.
Model / metric: Regenerated adsorption capacity / original capacity ratio (Qi/Q0×100%)
Evidence status: Extracted; metrics separated by experiment context
Caveat / follow-up: Ratio may exceed 100% if regenerated uptake rises; do not call it percent TC desorbed. No actual measured energy, kg-normalized consumption, real-water test, costs or LCA.

Experimental design / conditions: N2 BET/pore analysis, XRD, FTIR, SEM-EDS and TGA before/after TC adsorption and MW regeneration.
Reported result: BET area (m²/g): Sep 283.17 raw, 274.38 after TC, 224.00 after MW; Mt 45.52 raw, 41.83 after TC, 53.60 after MW. Pore volume/diameter recovered partly; FTIR TC-related bands weakened/disappeared after MW.
Caveat / follow-up: Surface-area recovery differs by mineral; reported continued performance is under lab batch conditions, not pilot-scale validation.

Experimental design / conditions: Review surveys pharmaceuticals in aqueous media, emphasizing montmorillonite, bentonite, kaolinite, palygorskite/sepiolite and modified clays. Table 2 summarizes contaminant, modifier, initial concentration, removal, kinetic/isotherm model, time, pH and temperature.
Reported result: The review describes montmorillonite as the most frequently discussed mineral in its table (8 entries) and highlights modification with surfactants, H2SO4/HCl or thermal treatment. It is a narrative overview; no reproducible search protocol or systematic flow diagram is reported in the main text.
Evidence status: Extracted from uploaded review main PDF
Caveat / follow-up: Use as context and citation-mining only; not a substitute for primary studies. The review covers non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals too, and its claims should not be described as a systematic review unless search methods are independently established.

Target / co-contaminant: Ciprofloxacin, amoxicillin, nalidixic acid, oxytetracycline, tetracycline, ampicillin, enrofloxacin, levofloxacin, gemifloxacin, clarithromycin
Adsorbent / material: Montmorillonite, bentonite, kaolinite, palygorskite/sepiolite; some surfactant/thermal modifications
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clays; selected modified-clay comparisons
Experimental design / conditions: Table 2 aggregates different primary studies and experimental regimes; feed concentrations mostly span mg/L to hundreds or thousands of mg/L.
Reported result: Examples reported by the review: bentonite/CIP 93.4–97.8% removal at 50–500 mg/L, pH 4.5, 30 min; bentonite/amoxicillin 97.9% at 50 mg/L with hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium modification, pH 7, 30 °C, 320 min; CTAB-bentonite/levofloxacin 90% at 30–250 mg/L and gemifloxacin 96% at 30–400 mg/L, pH 5, 24 h; montmorillonite/CIP 98% at 250 mg/L, 60 min, pH 7; montmorillonite/CIP in Wang et al. 2010: 97% removal at 500–4,000 mg/L, 24 h.
Value / units: % removal; C0 mg/L; time; pH; temperature
Evidence status: Secondary evidence, copied from review table
Caveat / follow-up: These are not directly comparable; one table cell may combine several contaminants. Verify the original cited paper before using any number in a quantitative comparison.

Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses kinetics, equilibrium/isotherms, thermodynamics and clay adsorbent types; its conclusion emphasizes pH/speciation and real-matrix competition.
Reported result: Authors report clay-based pharmaceutical removal up to 90–100% across cited studies, but emphasize that most studies use laboratory-prepared ultrapure-water solutions and that real effluents are under-studied. The review claims PSO often describes kinetics well and Langmuir/Freundlich often fit isotherms; fit quality alone does not establish mechanism.
Caveat / follow-up: No harmonized capacity ranking or economic/scale-up synthesis is provided. Use real-water gap as this review's observation, not a current field-wide count.

Target / co-contaminant: Doxycycline (Dxy), nitazoxanide (Ntx; described as antibiotic by the paper), and mixture SDN
Adsorbent / material: Waste PET-derived plastic char, KOH-activated carbon kC1170; PC and other activation variants as controls
Experimental design / conditions: PET bottles cut to ~1×1 mm; pyrolysed at 500 °C for 2 h under N2 with 10 °C/min ramp to make plastic char; activation by stirring in 1 M reagent solution for 2 h; KOH identified as best activator; optimized kC1170 uses KOH:PET 1:1 and carbonization temperature 700 °C, followed by 700 °C calcination for 120 min. Final washing/drying/grinding/sieving. Reported yield of kC1170 from PET waste is 25%.
Reported result: The process screens NaOH, HCl, H3PO4 and KOH activators, then 1:1 vs 2:1 KOH:PET and 300/500/700/900 °C carbonization choices. kC1170 selected as best overall compromise. Pilot scenario assumes 1 kg product from 4 kg PET waste.
Evidence status: Extracted from main PDF and Fig. 1 visually checked
Caveat / follow-up: Nitazoxanide is conventionally an antiparasitic agent rather than a standard antibiotic; keep its identity explicit. Product yield and process stages are author-reported; full SI inventory not retrieved.

Adsorbent / material: kC1170 vs PET char and KOH-activated carbons
Experimental design / conditions: SEM, N2 adsorption/desorption, XRD, EDS, FTIR, TGA and related characterization were used.
Reported result: kC1170 BET area 448.09 m²/g compared with 337.07 m²/g for plastic char; morphology shows porous/irregular layered structure; PZC 3.4. In the broader screening it also removed Congo red, sulfasalazine, DBT and Cr(VI).
Evidence status: Extracted from main PDF / figures inspected
Caveat / follow-up: This is not a pristine plastic char: it is chemically activated with KOH and subsequently calcined. Characterization/adsorption data depend on the chosen activation ratio and temperature.

Target / co-contaminant: Dxy and Ntx as single/mixture targets
Evidence domain: pH, dose, contact time and mass-balance check
Experimental design / conditions: Optimisation run: 25 °C; binary tests use stated Dxy/Ntx concentrations and dose as shown in Fig. 3–4 captions. Fig. 3d captions state 120 mg/L each, 1 g/L kC1170, pH 4 and 100 mL volume. Fig. 4 dose test states concentration 120 mg/L and doses 0.3–1.2 g/L.
Reported result: Authors report adsorption performance peaking at pH 3 (Dxy removal 89.58%; q≈107.5 mg/g) and report q values 246.3/267.5 mg/g for Dxy/Ntx at 0.3 g/L in the dose screen; at 1.0 g/L, reported removals 89.3/90.83% with q 87.21/89.66 mg/g. Fig. 3d appears to show ~170.2 mg/g for both targets with 120 mg/L initial concentration each and 1 g/L dose, which exceeds the single-target mass-balance ceiling of 120 mg/g; the q values in the dose section also do not align cleanly with removal×C0/dose. Flag as a reporting/condition inconsistency.
Model / metric: Observed values as reported; mass-balance audit
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–8; Figs. 3d and 4a–d, captions and text
Evidence status: Extracted; values flagged where inconsistent with stated conditions
Caveat / follow-up: Do not use questionable 170.2 mg/g or pair every q/removal as same-condition data until SI or source clarification resolves the mismatch. The abstract also prints one capacity unit as mg/L, whereas q is normally mass per adsorbent mass.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetics report 90% adsorption in 15 min and equilibrium by ~35 min under selected batch conditions. Isotherms at 15, 25 and 35 °C; Fig. 6 caption for binary tests states 100 mg/L of each antibiotic, 1 g/L sorbent, pH 4 and 50 min.
Reported result: Abstract-reported maximum capacities at 15 °C: Dxy 138.05 mg/g, Ntx 126.79 mg/g, SDN 324.75 mg/g. The main paper delegates detailed kinetic parameters to Table S2 and isotherm parameters to Table S3; those SI tables were not retrieved. Text reports the Langmuir–Freundlich model as best fit and lower capacities as temperature rises.
Evidence status: Main-text evidence extracted; SI parameters not available
Caveat / follow-up: Use capacities as author-reported provisional values and preserve the model/temperature label; no precise parameter table could be independently transcribed from the main PDF. Ntx category caveat remains.

Target / co-contaminant: Dxy, Ntx; other ions and natural water from GIK Institute, Swabi
Experimental design / conditions: Ion tests include Na+, K+, Ca2+, CO3²−, Cl− and NO3−; natural-water sample sourced from GIK Institute, Swabi. Fig. 6e caption uses 100 mg/L Dxy/Ntx each, 1 g/L dose, pH 4, 50 min; salt dose 0.15 mol/L.
Reported result: In natural water, reported removals were ~95% for Dxy and 67% for Ntx, compared with distilled-water removals 98.7% Dxy and 96.2% Ntx. NO3− caused the strongest listed inhibition of Ntx (removal 37.5%) but only marginal effect on Dxy (~97.6%). NaCl/CaCO3 ionic-strength increase depressed Ntx removal more sharply than Dxy.
Caveat / follow-up: Natural-water source is reported, but composition and representativeness are limited; this is not a fully characterized pharmaceutical wastewater validation. High salt doses of 0.15 M are controlled-ion tests, not necessarily realistic background levels.

Adsorbent / material: kC1170; ethanol wash, oven dry, 400 °C calcination
Experimental design / conditions: After initial adsorption, adsorbent washed with ethanol, dried at 90 °C and calcined at 400 °C; two-cycle results plotted in Fig. 6f.
Reported result: Authors report regeneration-cycle adsorption efficiencies around 72.5% for Dxy and 70.1% for Ntx after regeneration; after a second cycle, efficiencies declined to 38.2% and 35.5%, respectively.
Caveat / follow-up: Only short-cycle reuse is tested; no desorbed-antibiotic mass balance or transformation analysis. Calcination at 400 °C adds energy and emission considerations that should be included in sustainability comparisons.

Adsorbent / material: kC1170 surface and adsorbed molecular complexes
Experimental design / conditions: DFT binding structures, adsorption energy and reduced-density-gradient (RDG) analyses were used alongside FTIR/charge interpretation.
Reported result: Calculated adsorption energy: Dxy −16.90 kJ/mol, Ntx −11.75 kJ/mol, SDN −3.389 kJ/mol as reported; authors propose H-bonding and van der Waals interactions, with electrostatic effects in solution. Dxy shows stronger modeled affinity than Ntx; mixed adsorption adds steric hindrance.
Caveat / follow-up: DFT describes modeled interactions; it does not independently quantify the fraction of experimental uptake caused by each mechanism.

Target / co-contaminant: Production of 1 kg kC1170; environmental inventory
Adsorbent / material: PET waste, KOH, HCl, DI water, electricity
Experimental design / conditions: Attributional LCA using EcoInvent 3.1 background data and ReCiPe Midpoint method; functional output scaled to 1 kg kC1170. System includes collection, pre-processing, pyrolysis, activation, and post-processing. Excludes final disposal of spent kC1170, waste management during stages, use/application and handling/disposal of desorbed antibiotics.
Reported result: Reported 5.92 kg CO2-eq/kg kC1170; other reported indicators: 0.9464 kBq Co-60-eq ionizing radiation, 0.0304 kg NOx-eq ozone formation, 0.0070 kg PM2.5-eq, 0.0172 kg SO2-eq acidification, 0.0036 kg P-eq eutrophication, 98.50 kg 1,4-DCB-eq ecotoxicity, 12.27 kg 1,4-DCB-eq human toxicity, 0.0329 kg Cu-eq mineral scarcity, 1.75 kg oil-eq fossil scarcity, 0.0625 m³ water. KOH contributes 71.72% of impact contribution, PET 24.5%, water 2.54%, HCl 1.08%, energy 0.12%; stated process energy 24.04 MJ/kg.
Caveat / follow-up: Authors themselves call for more comprehensive LCA. Results are not cradle-to-grave and do not include spent media or adsorbed antibiotic fate.

Adsorbent / material: kC1170 from PET waste using KOH activation
Experimental design / conditions: ASPEN v11 pilot model; yield 25%; annual production scenario ~1,615 t; capital cost based on local costs in Pakistan. Costs include raw materials, utilities, labor, construction, maintenance and taxes, but details are in SI Tables S7–S10.
Reported result: Authors estimate US$13.75/kg product; capital investment approximately US$1.354 million; annual production cost ~US$20.95 million; revenue ~US$22 million; net profit ~US$0.85 million; stated ROI 63%, payback 1.6 years. Price compared against several commercial adsorbents.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 15–16; §3.8 and conclusion; SI Tables S7–S10 cited
Evidence status: Main-text values extracted; detailed spreadsheets/SI not retrieved
Caveat / follow-up: Costs are local to Pakistan and depend on assumptions; the paper itself says the comparison is preliminary and costs/burdens differ by adsorbent. Excluded disposal/use steps make the economic and environmental picture incomplete.

Target / co-contaminant: Tetracycline (TC), amoxicillin (Amox); residual metals V, Ni, Fe
Adsorbent / material: Sulfuric-acid-leached carbon-black refinery waste (LCBW); carbon black waste (CBW) precursor
Experimental design / conditions: CBW leached in 1 M H2SO4 at solid:liquid 0.1 g/mL, shaken 1 h, membrane-filtered, washed with DI water and dried at 105 °C. LCBW C 93.5%, H/N <0.5%, S 0.9%, O ~4.6–5.6%; BET in main results ~375 m²/g, average mesopore diameter 3.629 nm.
Reported result: Acid leaching reportedly reduced V from >16,000 to 400 ppm, Ni from >4,000 to 1,100 ppm and Fe to 600 ppm. Cd, Pb and As were not detected; other metals mostly <100 ppm. The main results report ~375 m²/g BET, but the conclusion says ~275 m²/g.
Evidence status: Extracted from main PDF and figures checked
Caveat / follow-up: BET-area inconsistency (375 vs ~275 m²/g) must remain flagged. Residual V/Ni/Fe remain present; soluble metal-leachate safety is inferred from prior work rather than a full release test in this study.

Evidence domain: Composite bead preparation and physical properties
Experimental design / conditions: 5 g LCBW dispersed in 190 mL 2% acetic acid and stirred 12 h; 4 g chitosan dissolved; gel rested 12 h then added dropwise into 1 M NaOH to gel; beads washed to pH 7.5–8.5.
Reported result: Bead density 1.287 g/mL; average diameter 3.56±0.6 mm; moisture content 94.1%; estimated LCBW content 20.5±0.5 mg per g composite bead; BET surface area of bead material ~20 m²/g and mean pore diameter 3.395 nm.
Value / units: mm; g/mL; % moisture; mg/g LCBW; m²/g
Caveat / follow-up: High bead moisture and low carbon loading help explain lower per-gram composite capacity versus powdered LCBW; beads prone to lose integrity below pH 5.

Experimental design / conditions: Batch adsorption at 22 °C, pH 7.5–8.5 except Amox in distilled water (pH fell by ~2 units). Powdered LCBW: TC feed 50 mg/L and final nominal dose appears 0.2 g/L from adding 0.2 g sorbent in 500 mL then an equal volume of TC solution; paper prose also says 0.4 g/L. Powder Amox: 25 mg/L with reported 0.4 g/L. Beads: TC/Amox 25 mg/L, 20 g/L beads for TC and 10 g/L for Amox.
Reported result: Table 5: powder TC removal 68% distilled/80% tap; powder Amox 72%/91%; beads TC 92%/87%; beads Amox 62%/74%. Table 6 capacities: powder TC 181 mg/g distilled/205 tap; beads TC 39/38; powder Amox 42/65; beads Amox 12/15 mg/g.
Model / metric: Observed removal and empirical capacity; different doses/feeds
Caveat / follow-up: The method's stated LCBW dosage for TC is internally ambiguous after doubling solution volume; capacity values roughly align with 0.2 g/L rather than the prose's 0.4 g/L. Preserve the source ambiguity and don't harmonize without the authors' data.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetics in distilled/tap water at pH 7.5–8.5 and 22 °C; feeds 50 mg/L TC or 25 mg/L Amox for powder; beads at 25 mg/L target. Experiments in duplicate; reported maximum experimental error ±5%.
Reported result: Most uptake occurred in the first 7 h; equilibrium around 24 h except Amox on powder. PSO fit for powder TC R² >0.999; powder Amox PSO R² 0.885–0.977. For composite beads, PFO fit R² >0.995. Intraparticle diffusion plots have multiple linear segments and do not pass origin, so it was not the sole rate-limiting step.
Caveat / follow-up: Kinetic-model fit should not be treated as standalone proof of chemisorption. Tap-water ion effects differ between powder and composite beads.

Experimental design / conditions: Glass column with tap water; bed heights 6.5, 10.5, 14.5 cm; flows 1 or 2 mL/min; initial TC concentrations approximately 49.2 or 51.8 mg/L. Breakthrough discussed at C/C0 = 0.1.
Reported result: Breakthrough and time increased with bed height. At 14.5 cm, estimated time to C/C0=0.1 was ~60 h at 1 mL/min vs ~25 h at 2 mL/min. Table 7 model-derived Thomas capacities q were 5.051–8.757 mg/g; Adams–Bohart R² 0.795–0.969 and Thomas gave nearly identical predictions, but authors say neither fit was satisfactory.
Value / units: cm; mL/min; h; modelled mg/g; R²
Caveat / follow-up: The model estimates should not be treated as validated dynamic service capacities: authors explicitly say Adams–Bohart and Thomas fits are inadequate. No pilot-scale or real wastewater test.

Experimental design / conditions: XPS identifies C–C/C=C, C–OH/C–O–C, C=O/C–N and O–C=O/N=C–O groups; FTIR of beads shows O–H/N–H, C–H, amide I/II/III and C–O–C bands. Tap water pH 7.9; contains Ca 50.5, Mg 5.0, Na 23.9, K 3.8, bicarbonate 132 mg/L and other ions as Table 2.
Reported result: Authors propose hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interaction, π–π/hydrophobic interactions and surface bridging/complexation. Tap-water cations improve powder adsorption (TC 68→80%, Amox 72→91%) but effects on beads are weaker or opposite (TC 92→87%, Amox 62→74%).
Caveat / follow-up: The paper presents LCBW as cost-effective but does not quantify the unit production cost, regenerate the beads in this study, or conduct a full leaching/LCA assessment. Residual metals and bead stability remain practical questions.

Adsorbent / material: Oxytetracycline fermentation residue-derived, in-situ N-doped KOH-activated biochar AOBC-3–600; POBC and UAOBC-600 controls
Continuum stage: Stage 3/4 — activated, in-situ N-doped biochar from pharmaceutical waste
Experimental design / conditions: OFR dry at 105 °C, grind to 60 mesh; pre-carbonize at 400 °C for 2 h under N2 at 2 °C/min, wash and dry 80 °C; mix POBC:KOH 1:3; pyrolyse at 600 °C for 1 h under N2 at 2 °C/min; wash with 0.1 M HCl then DI water to neutral; dry 80 °C.
Reported result: Authors repurpose nitrogen-rich fermentation residue as both carbon precursor and in-situ N source, avoiding a separately added external N-dopant source. Product yield and full reagent/water/energy balance are not reported.
Evidence status: Extracted from uploaded main PDF; SI Table S1 not retrieved
Caveat / follow-up: KOH ratio optimization is in SI; no product yield, energy consumption, wash-water or waste-acid cost in main text.

Experimental design / conditions: N2 adsorption-desorption, SEM, XRD, FTIR, XPS and elemental analysis; Fig. 1 shows pore distribution/isotherm; Figs. 2–4 show morphology and spectra.
Reported result: BET surface area: POBC 2.41 m²/g, UAOBC-600 6.37 m²/g, AOBC-3–600 1960.38 m²/g; reported microporosity 61.6%, pore diameter mainly 0–2 nm; AOBC nitrogen 5.80 wt%, O/C <0.6 and C/H atomic ratio 31.76.
Evidence status: Extracted; detailed elemental table is SI-dependent
Caveat / follow-up: Exceptional area is for strongly KOH-activated material, not raw biomass biochar; no yield or cost accompanies the area value.

Experimental design / conditions: General batch protocol: 20 mL, C0 10–100 mg/L, dose 0.125–2 g/L, pH 2–10, 180 rpm, 24 h, 25 °C, dark. Dose graph conditions: 100 mg/L, 24 h, 25 °C.
Reported result: From 0.125 to 2 g/L, removal increased TC 36.87→79.06%, CTC 41.72→98.84%, OTC 57.43→100%, DOC 36.74→99.55%. At 0.125 g/L, reported capacities were TC 294.93, CTC 333.77, OTC 459.48 and DOC 293.89 mg/g; capacities per gram fell toward ~50 mg/g at 2 g/L as adsorbent dose increased.
Evidence status: Extracted from main-text figure and narrative
Caveat / follow-up: High removal at high dose is not identical to qmax; dose study uses high 100 mg/L antibiotic concentration and synthetic solution.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm methods: 20 mL antibiotic, C0 100–500 mg/L, 0.005 g adsorbent (0.25 g/L), 180 rpm, 24 h, at 25, 35 and 45 °C.
Reported result: Abstract/conclusion report Langmuir-model maximum capacities at 25 °C: TC 473.00 mg/g, CTC 293.28 mg/g, OTC 220.61 mg/g and DOC 282.72 mg/g.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1, 3, 8–10; Fig. 7; Table S6 cited
Evidence status: Main-text abstract/conclusion extraction; fit table not present
Caveat / follow-up: Full Langmuir/Freundlich parameters, errors and R² are in missing SI Table S6. Do not label these as observed q at a single concentration.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, CTC, OTC, DOC; pH and common ions
Experimental design / conditions: pH study: 100 mg/L, 0.5 g/L, pH 2–10, 25 °C, 24 h. Kinetic study: 0.055 g in 110 mL of 100 mg/L antibiotic, pH 5, 25 °C, 180 rpm, samples from 5–1440 min. Common-ion tests at 100 mg/L, 0.5 g/L and pH 5.
Reported result: Capacity optima: TC pH 3, CTC pH 2, OTC pH 2, DOC pH 9. Fast uptake phase accounts for 97.37% TC, 91.17% OTC, 78.84% CTC and 53.97% DOC reported total removal; OTC uptake is described as complete at 600 min. CO3²−/HCO3−/PO4³− reportedly had little effect; Na+/K+ slightly promoted uptake, while Ca²+/Mg²+ inhibited it.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 6–9; Fig. 5d–f; §§3.2.3–3.5; Fig. S2 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Multiple protocols in Fig. 5 have different C0 (100 mg/L and a 500 mg/L temperature panel); keep these separate. SI Table S4 kinetic values not retrieved.

Experimental design / conditions: FTIR and XPS before/after adsorption, pH response, kinetics and isotherm models; intraparticle diffusion described using a three-stage fit in SI.
Reported result: Authors propose pore filling, electrostatic attraction, H-bonding, π–π and Lewis acid–base interaction. PSO R² reported 0.9486–0.9970 vs PFO R² 0.9167–0.9851. Intraparticle diffusion stages: rapid external surface uptake, diffusion into internal pores, then near-equilibrium saturation.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–9; Figs. 6–8; Tables S4–S6 and Fig. S1 cited
Evidence status: Mechanism interpretation extracted from main text
Caveat / follow-up: PSO fit is not proof of chemisorption. Printed equations on PDF p. 3 use Ce−C0 in q and removal formulas, apparently reversing the normal sign; flag as likely typographical error.

Target / co-contaminant: Residual OTC and four resistance genes: tet(A), tet(C), tet(M), tet(O)
Experimental design / conditions: Regeneration with 0.1 M NaOH until no TCs detected in solution; five adsorption/desorption cycles. OTC leaching: 0–2 g/L AOBC-3–600 in 20 mL DI water, 180 rpm, 24 h, 25 °C; filtrate checked by UV–Vis. Four tet genes assessed by PCR/qPCR and gel electrophoresis.
Reported result: Authors report removal rate declining by only about 4% after five cycles; Table 1 lists reusability/removal figures of 96.90% TC, 89.23% CTC, 95.08% OTC and 95.44% DOC but does not make cycle mapping fully clear. Filtrate absorbance did not exceed DI-water control; no bands for four tested tet genes were found.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4, 9–10; Table 1; §3.7; Tables S7 and Fig. S4 cited
Evidence status: Main-text results; cycle mapping/safety details partly unresolved
Caveat / follow-up: No detectable signal under these assays does not prove absence of all antibiotics/resistance genes or universal safety; four genes only; no real wastewater or leachate toxicity test.

Adsorbent / material: Biochars from shell, agricultural/forestry residue, sludge and manure feedstocks
Experimental design / conditions: Review Table 1 compiles TC maximum capacities across many original papers; different precursor, pyrolysis condition and solution condition are used.
Reported result: Review-reported examples (mg/g): crayfish-shell 39.10; pomelo peel 14.42; Camellia oleifera shell 13.85; rice straw 150.20; straw 65.80; tea waste 16.71; Fraxinus marsh leaves 60.78; lignin 277.7; aerobic granular sludge 15.01; cassava ethanol sludge 34.04; pharmaceutical sludge 94.69; sewage sludge 89.30; swine manure 127.80; bovine manure 5.82.
Evidence status: Secondary evidence; original papers not checked individually here
Caveat / follow-up: Not an apples-to-apples ranking; confirm conditions and fitted versus measured capacity against the primary paper before using numbers in the manuscript.

Experimental design / conditions: Review compares high-temperature pyrolysis, microwave pyrolysis and hydrothermal liquefaction; describes physical (steam, heat, ball milling), chemical (acid/base, oxidant, metal salt/oxide, clay/organic reagent) and biological modification.
Reported result: Review summarizes common conventional pyrolysis at roughly 300–800 °C and compares temperature/time/yield trade-offs. Its Table 2 reports example yield ranges of about 15–50% for high-temperature pyrolysis (depending on speed/conditions), 30–50% for microwave pyrolysis and 40–60% for hydrothermal liquefaction.
Caveat / follow-up: Values are representative literature summaries rather than universal process yields; feedstock and reactor boundaries differ.

Experimental design / conditions: Review surveys pH/speciation, co-existing ions, temperature, humic acid/organic matter, initial concentration and dose.
Reported result: Possible mechanisms summarized: pore filling, H-bonding, π–π electron donor–acceptor interactions, electrostatic interactions, Lewis acid–base interactions, surface complexation and cation exchange. Humic acid can inhibit uptake through competition or sometimes increase uptake by bridging/new-site effects.
Caveat / follow-up: These are possible mechanisms from heterogeneous primary studies, not universal mechanisms for every biochar/TC system.

Target / co-contaminant: TC in real wastewater, sewage, tap and river water
Continuum stage: Review / practical matrix and regeneration source mining
Experimental design / conditions: Examples summarized in review include different real or semi-real water matrices and several regeneration protocols; cited originals use separate conditions.
Reported result: Review-reported examples: Zn-loaded BC capacities 52.65 and 85.64 mg/g in two sewage types; phosphorus-containing high-mesoporosity BC lowered TOC 53.2→18.4 mg/L in medical-production wastewater; banana-peel BC gave about 96% TC removal in industrial TC/Pb wastewater; one study reported ~180 mg/g TC uptake in tap/river water. Review says many studies retain performance over ~2–5 reuse cycles.
Evidence status: Secondary evidence; original sources need retrieval
Caveat / follow-up: TOC is not a target-specific TC-removal metric. Verify each citation, water matrix, C0, dose and whether values are observed or fitted before quantitative use.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics on biomass-derived biochar and activated carbon
Adsorbent / material: Biochar and activated carbon from biomass
Experimental design / conditions: Search databases/resources: Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Scopus and ResearchGate; stated window 2015 through 30 April 2024. Search strings include “Biochar and activated carbon for antibiotic adsorption” and “biochar AND activated AND carbon AND antibiotic OR pharmaceutical AND adsorption”.
Reported result: Fig. 1 reports 451 Web of Science + 4,995 ScienceDirect + 107 Scopus + 48 ResearchGate = 5,601 records; 3,054 after deduplication, 632 screened for content, 359 full texts assessed, 305 included in qualitative assessment and 162 studies in the SLR. The diagram also lists 54 full-text exclusions.
Evidence status: Extracted from uploaded review; count ambiguity flagged
Caveat / follow-up: 305 qualitative-assessment studies vs 162 final included and 54 stated full-text exclusions do not fully reconcile; the displayed database query also lacks parentheses around OR logic. Do not quote one final count as reconciled.

Adsorbent / material: Biochar and activated carbon from biomass
Experimental design / conditions: Review analyses literature collected through April 2024. It compares one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT), design of experiments (DoE), response surface methodology (RSM) and Taguchi approaches.
Reported result: Review states 2023 had the highest annual number in its chart (74), followed by 2022 (58), 2021 (52), 2020 (20), 2019 (14), 2018 (6) and 2015 (1); about 62 papers were already recorded in 2024 first quarter. It argues DoE/RSM yields more efficient and informative multi-factor optimization than OFAT/Taguchi in its synthesis.
Evidence status: Secondary evidence; study-count context not fully reconciled
Caveat / follow-up: The paper elsewhere refers to 301 articles while Fig. 1 reports 162 in the SLR; chart counts and the search flow should be treated cautiously. RSM is not universally superior for every experimental aim.

Adsorbent / material: Biochar and activated carbon; Fe/Ti biochar, pomegranate-peel BC, brewery-waste AC
Experimental design / conditions: Review summarizes multiple primary studies comparing simulated/synthetic and actual water matrices.
Reported result: Review-reported examples: Fe/Ti biochar composite removal for norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin fell about 10% in Nanming River water versus synthetic water; pomegranate-peel BC CIP removal 96.31% synthetic vs 89.94% real for batch, and 94.39% synthetic vs 84.74% real for column; brewery-waste AC removal of SMX/TMP/CIP 36/64/56% versus 42/84/78% after oxygen functionalization.
Caveat / follow-up: Use as prioritized citation leads only; exact water chemistry, C0, doses, matrix and experimental design must be extracted from original papers before any direct comparison.

Adsorbent / material: Walnut shell BC, pomegranate-peel BC, PET-AC-ZFO and other carbons
Experimental design / conditions: Review describes HCl/solvent elution, NaOH, acetic acid, ultrasound and reuse experiments across separate studies.
Reported result: Examples reported: walnut-shell BC reused for sulfonamide adsorption after five desorption treatments/four reuse cycles; pomegranate-peel BC CIP removal reached 81.27% at the fifth cycle; PET-AC-ZFO retained over 58% efficiency through six tetracycline cycles. Values are based on different cycle metrics and protocols.
Evidence status: Secondary evidence; primary protocols not rechecked here
Caveat / follow-up: Do not harmonize cycles across adsorbents; retained removal percentage is not the same as fraction of adsorbate desorbed.

Target / co-contaminant: Biomass biochar / activated carbon production cost
Experimental design / conditions: Table 4 aggregates reported prices from studies in different years/locations; not a common techno-economic boundary.
Reported result: Historical price examples in review: coconut-shell biochar US$0.80/kg; coconut-shell AC US$1.50–3.00/kg; granular AC US$6.40/kg; virgin-wood biochar US$17.80/kg; sludge biochar US$0.70/kg; HCl-modified BC US$0.69/kg; Si-modified BC US$1.44/kg; chitosan-AC US$15.40/kg; Filtrasorb-400 US$20–22/kg; commercial AC US$21/kg.
Caveat / follow-up: Not current comparable quotations; year, scale, energy prices, feedstock credit/subsidy and production boundaries vary. Retrieve originals before economic comparison.

Evidence domain: Synthesis of mechanisms, regeneration and scale-up gaps
Experimental design / conditions: Review examines pH, concentration, dose, temperature, surface properties, ionic strength, real matrices, adsorption/column behavior and the cost of production/operation.
Reported result: Mechanisms summarized: H-bonding, van der Waals, electrostatic attraction/repulsion, π–π interaction, pore filling and complexation. Practical constraints include matrix competition, material variability/leaching, regenerant waste, stability, cost and limited use-stage/end-of-life assessment.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not treat a mechanism named in the review as independently proven for any specific adsorbent; trace to source spectroscopy/competition/speciation evidence.

Adsorbent / material: Five natural clay powders: Archidona, Blanca, Esquivias, Negra, Yuncos
Experimental design / conditions: XRF, N2 physisorption and CEC measurements; powders compared for TC retention. Table 1 lists SBET 135, 39, 257, 21 and 58 m²/g; pore volumes 0.169, 0.079, 0.224, 0.042 and 0.102 cm³/g; available CEC values 42, n.a., 15, n.a., and 109 meq/100 g in the same order.
Reported result: Esquivias kerolitic montmorillonite selected for honeycomb monolith production based on TC retention plus its mesoporous structure and high surface area; authors note area alone does not determine capacity, as Yuncos can outperform Archidona despite lower area.
Caveat / follow-up: Not all clay CEC values are reported; raw clay properties are not directly comparable to processed biochars/carbon materials without conditions and matrix details.

Experimental design / conditions: Table 4 reports TC removed per gram of clay under light/air at 25 °C, with pH 3/7/9. Separate Esquivias pH/temperature test protocols are discussed in §3.1.
Reported result: Table 4 values (mg/g) at pH 3/7/9 respectively: Archidona 85.4/24.2/42.2; Blanca 12.1/6.1/37.4; Esquivias 102.4/80.5/80.2; Negra 33.7/23.0/42.1; Yuncos 81.2/30.0/49.2. Separate Esquivias discussion reports 64.2 and 64.8 mg/g at pH 3/9 versus 79 mg/g at pH 7; 72 mg/g at 4 °C and 116.8 mg/g at 60 °C.
Model / metric: Reported retained amount per clay mass, condition-specific
Evidence status: Extracted; differing test protocols retained separately
Caveat / follow-up: Do not merge the separate pH/temperature series with Table 4; higher-temperature apparent removal may include TC degradation. Spectra shift with pH and require pH-specific calibration.

Experimental design / conditions: Paste used 0.42 mL water per g clay; extruded monolith diameter 1.4 cm, 50 cells/cm², wall 0.33 mm, frontal open area 72%; calcined at 400 °C for 2 h. Calcined powder SBET about 220 m²/g; type-II isotherm/H3 hysteresis with pore distribution centered on ~4 nm.
Reported result: Monoliths are designed to ease recovery/handling and avoid sludge associated with powder; three tests used monolith masses 3.14/4.20/3.43 g and initial TC around 231–460 ppm in 500/335/2000 mL with different light/air/flow conditions.
Caveat / follow-up: Calcination energy and product yield/cost are not quantified in a harmonized TEA/LCA.

Experimental design / conditions: Tests at pH 7; example setup: 4.2 g monolith, 335 mL at TC 231 mg/L, 50 mL/min recirculation. Other configurations used no forced flow or 2800 mL/min, with different volumes/air/light and longer durations.
Reported result: At 50 mL/min, up to 69% removal reported after 3 days recirculation. Authors also report 80% with no forced circulation and 82% at 2800 mL/min, but these configurations have differing exposure times and are explicitly not directly comparable.
Model / metric: Recirculation tests, not once-through column capacity
Caveat / follow-up: High feed (~231 ppm) and recirculation mode; do not describe as trace-level real-wastewater or pilot once-through demonstration.

Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clay / separate regeneration operation
Experimental design / conditions: UV–Vis, zeta potential, XRD and TPO; monoliths calcined at 400 °C for 2 h during fabrication. Post-use TPO under oxygen identified H2O/CO2 signals and TC-associated decomposition broadly across 200–600 °C.
Reported result: Authors infer surface/mesopore adsorption with cation exchange and pH effects; XRD changes little after TC treatment, suggesting negligible interlayer intercalation in this system. They propose post-use heating around 300–350 °C for 1–2 h to decompose much of retained TC and reuse the monolith.
Model / metric: Adsorption evidence plus separate thermal destruction inference
Caveat / follow-up: Do not count post-use heating as adsorption removal or assert complete mineralization solely from H2O/CO2 signals; full product/toxicity mass balance not provided; no detailed TEA/LCA.

Adsorbent / material: Review across activated carbon, waste-derived sorbents, graphene oxide, zeolites/clays/silica, MOFs and composites
Experimental design / conditions: Review synthesizes HWW characteristics, antibiotics, adsorption materials, matrix effects and scale-up. HWW is described as a complex mixture of pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, metals, microbes/pathogens and other contaminants.
Reported result: Review quotes cross-study concentration ranges of approximately 0.04–17.9 μg/L antibiotics in HWW versus 0.03–1.75 μg/L in municipal WWTP effluents. It emphasizes hospital-to-hospital/regional variability and importance of source treatment.
Model / metric: Secondary review of reported environmental occurrence
